01 DATABASE + ANALYTICS PROJECT

What happens between placing an order and food arriving at the doorstep?

I analyzed the operational backbone of a digital food delivery marketplace using relational data across customers, restaurants, menu items, orders, couriers, and deliveries. The goal was to understand how the platform performs end to end — from customer spending to delivery efficiency.

What did I want to understand?

01 — CUSTOMERS

Who creates the most value?

02 — RESTAURANTS

03 — COURIERS

02 DATABASE STRUCTURE

Modeling the full order lifecycle

The relational schema connects the customer experience to the operational work happening behind the scenes. Customers place orders, restaurants publish menu items, order items capture the products purchased, and deliveries connect fulfilled orders to delivery partners.

CUSTOMERS

Demand

Identity, activity, and location support segmentation and lifecycle analysis.

ORDERS

Transactions

The central transaction table captures demand, fees, revenue, and fulfillment outcomes.

RESTAURANTS

Supply

Restaurants, menu items, and order items represent the purchasing funnel.

DELIVERIES

Fulfillment

Courier assignment, pickup/drop-off timing, tips, and cost connect operations to service quality.

Key relationships. Each order belongs to exactly one customer, while a customer can place zero to many orders. Each delivery is handled by exactly one delivery partner, while a partner can complete zero to many deliveries. Together, the schema supports analysis across customer acquisition, restaurant supply, transaction processing, item-level sales, courier execution, and marketplace service quality.

04 DELIVERY PARTNER PERFORMANCE

How much does delivery speed vary by courier?

One of the clearest operational questions was identifying the fastest and slowest delivery partners. I calculated average delivery time from pickup to drop-off and compared performance across completed deliveries.

Average delivery time by partner

The query calculates delivery duration in minutes and ranks partners from fastest to slowest.

SQL
SELECT
    dp.dp_id,
    dp.name,
    ROUND(
        AVG((julianday(d.dropoff_time) - julianday(d.pickup_time)) * 24 * 60),
        2
    ) AS avg_delivery_minutes,
    COUNT(d.delivery_id) AS total_deliveries
FROM delivery_partners dp
JOIN deliveries d ON dp.dp_id = d.dp_id
WHERE d.pickup_time IS NOT NULL
  AND d.dropoff_time IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY dp.dp_id, dp.name
ORDER BY avg_delivery_minutes ASC;
✦   Key finding

Delivery speed varied clearly across partners. Patty Holt, Shelley Lucas, and Bridget Summers averaged roughly 22–23 minutes per delivery, while Luke Peterson, Randy Kent, Joseph Lopez, and Martha Torres were closer to 27 minutes — a gap of about five minutes.

Why this matters. Even a relatively small delivery-time gap can influence customer satisfaction, repeat ordering, and perceptions of reliability. This analysis can help identify high-performing couriers, investigate inefficiencies, improve dispatching decisions, and monitor service quality.

05 CUSTOMER SPENDING

Customer value is more than order count

To understand customer contribution, I calculated the full cost of each customer's orders rather than looking only at food subtotal. The analysis combines item prices and quantities with delivery fees and tips.

Building total customer spend

Layered CTEs connect order items, orders, and deliveries before aggregating to the customer level.

SQL
WITH customer_payment_info AS (
    WITH order_price_info AS (
        SELECT
            oi.item_price_at_order,
            oi.quantity,
            oi.order_id,
            o.customer_id,
            d.tip_amount,
            o.delivery_fee
        FROM order_items oi
        LEFT JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
        LEFT JOIN deliveries d ON oi.order_id = d.order_id
    )
    SELECT
        customer_id,
        tip_amount,
        delivery_fee,
        SUM(item_price_at_order * quantity) AS order_total
    FROM order_price_info
    GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT
    customer_id,
    SUM(tip_amount + delivery_fee + order_total) AS customer_total
FROM customer_payment_info
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
✦   Key finding

Customer value is not just about how often someone orders. Total spend becomes more informative when the food subtotal, delivery fee, and tip are considered together.

06 MACHINE LEARNING

Predicting delivery time

I extended the project beyond descriptive analytics by framing a regression problem around delivery duration. The goal was to approximate how long a delivery would take and understand which variables were most strongly associated with delays.

MODELLasso

Regression with standardized features

Delivery timeGeographyDistanceOperations
EXPECTATION

Distance

I initially expected distance to be the strongest driver of delivery time.

RESULT

Boston

The strongest positive coefficient was associated with being in Boston rather than raw distance.

INTERPRETATION

Context matters

Geographic context appeared to capture operational complexity that distance alone did not explain.

↗
Unexpected insight

Geographic context appeared to matter more than raw distance alone. A likely explanation is omitted-variable bias: traffic, road design, parking difficulty, and urban density were not represented directly in the model.

This reinforced an important analytics lesson: the most intuitive variable is not always the most explanatory one. In operational settings, hidden complexity can shape outcomes more than a simple measure such as distance.

07 TAKEAWAYS

What I learned from the marketplace

01 — SYSTEM VIEW

Analyze the full lifecycle

Food delivery is better understood as a connected system than as isolated transactions.

02 — SQL

Operational patterns emerge

Relational analysis makes courier performance and customer value measurable across entities.

03 — MODELING

Prediction exposes hidden drivers

Even an imperfect model can reveal factors that deserve deeper operational investigation.

Limitations

The model and dataset leave room for more targeted future analysis.

DATA10 months

The dataset was too short to evaluate full-year seasonality.

FEATURESToo broad

Too many features made the model more generic and less interpretable.

SEGMENTSMixed contexts

Insufficient segmentation reduced prediction accuracy.

OPERATIONSMissing context

Traffic, street layout, parking, and density were not directly modeled.

Recommended next steps

Future modeling should narrow the prediction context and add operational features.

Add time-of-day and day-of-week features, segment deliveries into more homogeneous groups, build context-specific models such as city-based or bike-only deliveries, and incorporate traffic or street-layout variables where possible. A stronger future question would be: How long will a New York bike delivery take on a Friday night at 6 PM?

Final reflection

This project showed me how structured relational data can be transformed into a business story. Combining database design, SQL analysis, and predictive modeling made it possible to examine the marketplace across customers, restaurants, and couriers — and connect technical analysis back to operational decisions.
